screens.title: Aggregation and Grouping with GROUP BY and HAVING
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how S Q L turns raw rows into meaningful summaries. Aggregation is the set of techniques—COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX—that let you compress many rows into single summary values. Grouping splits rows into categories so those aggregates apply per category. Finally, HAVING lets you filter those categories using conditions on aggregate results. These tools answer questions like “what is total revenue per category?” or “which customers placed more than three orders and spent over five hundred dollars?” You will see concrete S Q L examples and a short hands-on activity using PageViews. We'll also clarify a common confusion: WHERE filters rows before aggregation, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Understanding the order of execution—FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY—helps you write correct queries and avoid errors such as trying to use SUM inside WHERE. By the end, you'll be able to produce grouped reports and choose whether a condition belongs in WHERE or HAVING. Think of aggregation as turning many measurements into the single insight that informs decisions—what summary do you need to answer your question?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Aggregation & Grouping
Aggregation and Grouping with GROUP BY and HAVING
Summarize rows, group by meaningful keys, and filter grouped summaries.
In this lesson

Learn the five core aggregate functions and how GROUP BY creates groups for per-category summaries. Learn to use HAVING to filter groups after aggregates are computed.

Why it matters

Aggregation is how reports, dashboards, and many analytics queries produce actionable insights from raw event and transaction data.

Explore Key Topics
Aggregate Functions
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX to summarize rows.
GROUP BY
Split rows into groups so aggregates apply per group.
HAVING
Filter groups using aggregate conditions after grouping.
Concept Map
Rows → Groups → Aggregates → Group Filters. Use WHERE before grouping; HAVING after.
COUNT
Row counts and distinct counts.
SUM / AVG
Totals and averages for numeric analysis.
MIN / MAX
Earliest, latest, smallest, or largest values.
HAVING
Filter groups based on aggregate results.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
This lesson uses a code-first live-coding style. Expect examples that start with a Sales or PageViews table, show aggregates across the whole table, then add GROUP BY, WHERE, and HAVING to demonstrate the change in results.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will confidently summarize data with standard aggregate functions, group rows into meaningful categories using GROUP BY, apply HAVING to filter grouped summaries, and explain when to use WHERE versus HAVING. You will be able to choose COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, or MAX based on the question you need to answer. For example, you will write queries that report total revenue per product category, count unique users per region, or find the latest event per device. We include short mnemonics and competency milestones so you can self-check: start by applying aggregates to a whole table, then group by one or more columns, then add HAVING to exclude groups that don't meet criteria. These skills matter because most analytics and reporting tasks rely on correct aggregation and grouping. Practicing the provided example queries and the PageViews task will verify that you can build grouped reports and avoid common mistakes like placing aggregate conditions in WHERE. Aim to reach the verified competency milestone by producing accurate grouped results that match the expected summaries.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Validation
screens.narratorSegment: This screen gives you practical validation steps. First, verify you can compute aggregates over the entire table: run COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX and check each result against known values or simple calculations. Second, test GROUP BY by grouping data by a single column and confirming that non-aggregated columns you select are listed in GROUP BY. Third, apply HAVING to exclude groups using aggregate conditions and check the counts and sums that remain. A common validation technique is to run the query without GROUP BY and then with GROUP BY on a small data subset to compare results manually. Another useful check is deliberately moving a condition between WHERE and HAVING to observe changes — for example, filter orders by date in WHERE and then require SUM(total_amount) > 500 in HAVING. These steps ensure you choose the right clause and that your aggregates reflect the intended scope of rows. Finally, reflect on one real report you build and identify which conditions are row-level and which are group-level before you write the query.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Practice & Validation
Validation checklist
  • Run each aggregate over the whole table and confirm totals and averages match expectations.
  • When adding GROUP BY, ensure every non-aggregated SELECT column is in GROUP BY.
  • Use HAVING to filter by aggregates and WHERE to filter raw rows before grouping.
  • Test queries on small data subsets to manually verify grouped results.
Quick mnemonic
Where filters rows. Having filters groups. Aggregate happens after grouping.

screens.title: Aggregate Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
screens.narratorSegment: Aggregate functions compute a single summary value from multiple rows. COUNT returns the number of rows or the number of non-null values in a column; COUNT(DISTINCT) limits to unique non-null values. SUM adds numeric values and is the primary tool for totals such as total revenue. AVG gives the arithmetic mean and is useful for understanding typical values like average order value. MIN and MAX find the smallest or largest value in a set, which is helpful for earliest dates or highest prices. Use aggregates without GROUP BY when you want a single summary for the entire filtered dataset. For example, SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM Orders calculates the grand total of orders. Keep in mind null handling: COUNT(column) ignores nulls while COUNT(*) counts every row. A common misconception is thinking AVG ignores nulls differently across databases; in practice AVG operates on the non-null values present in the set. Concrete example: in a Sales table, SUM(sale_amount) gives total revenue, AVG(sale_amount) gives the average sale, and MAX(sale_date) finds the most recent sale date. Key takeaway: pick the aggregate that matches the question you ask—total, average, count, earliest, or latest.

keyIdea.title: Aggregate summary
keyIdea.text: Choose the aggregate that matches your question: count rows, sum totals, average values, or find min/max values.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Aggregate Functions
Aggregate Functions
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — single-value summaries from sets of rows.
Definitions
  • COUNT() counts rows or non-null values; COUNT(DISTINCT) counts unique values.
  • SUM() adds numeric values to produce totals.
  • AVG() computes the mean of numeric values (non-null values only).
  • MIN()/MAX() find smallest and largest values, including dates.
Concrete example
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
  SUM(total_amount) AS total_revenue,
  AVG(total_amount) AS avg_order_value,
  MIN(order_date) AS first_order,
  MAX(order_date) AS last_order
FROM Orders;
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use the aggregate that directly answers your analytic question and be mindful of how nulls and DISTINCT affect counts and averages.

Common misconception

A frequent mistake is assuming COUNT(column) equals COUNT(*) when NULL values exist. COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, so it can be smaller. Also, DISTINCT changes COUNT to unique non-null values only.

Try this
Run each aggregate on your table first, then add GROUP BY to see how results break down by category.

screens.title: COUNT variations and NULL behavior
screens.narratorSegment: COUNT is deceptively simple but has important variants. COUNT(*) counts every row in the result set, including rows where some columns are NULL. COUNT(column_name) counts only non-null values in that column. COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) counts unique non-null values. These differences matter when columns can be NULL or when you care about unique entities. For example, if you want to know how many orders exist, use COUNT(*) or COUNT(order_id) assuming order_id is never null; to count distinct customers who ordered, use COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). A common error is using COUNT(column) to count rows when that column can be NULL, which undercounts results. Also, using COUNT(DISTINCT) adds uniqueness semantics that can change the meaning of the metric: distinct page URLs visited versus total page views. Concrete example: in a PageViews table, COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) tells you how many different pages each user visited, while COUNT(page_url) gives total views. Key takeaway: pick the COUNT variant that captures the exact measure you want and be explicit about NULL and uniqueness semantics. COUNT variations and NULL behavior means count(*) counts rows; count(column) ignores nulls; count(distinct) counts unique non-null values—pick the one that matches your metric.. In practical terms, count(*), count(column), and count(distinct) explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › COUNT Variations
COUNT forms
  • COUNT(*) — counts all rows returned.
  • COUNT(column_name) — counts non-null values in that column.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) — counts unique non-null values.
-- Example: distinct pages visited per user and total views
SELECT
  user_id,
  COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) AS distinct_pages,
  COUNT(page_url) AS total_page_views
FROM PageViews
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) > 10
ORDER BY total_page_views DESC;
Practical note

When a column can be NULL, COUNT(column) will be lower than COUNT(*). Confirm whether your identifier column allows NULLs before choosing which COUNT to use.

Common mistake
Watch out

Using COUNT(column) to mean total rows when column contains NULLs will produce an undercount. Use COUNT(*) for total rows.

screens.title: SUM and AVG for numeric summaries
screens.narratorSegment: SUM and AVG are the primary tools for numeric summaries. SUM adds values across rows to produce a total such as total sales or total bytes transferred. AVG computes the average of non-null values and is useful for understanding typical order sizes, session lengths, or ratings. Use SUM when you need a cumulative measure and AVG when you need a central tendency. Keep in mind that AVG's value depends on which rows are included: include or exclude rows with WHERE before grouping to change the average’s domain. A common misconception is treating AVG as resistant to outliers; it is sensitive to extreme values, so sometimes a median or trimmed average is more appropriate — though median is not a standard aggregate in every S Q L dialect. Concrete example: average order value per customer is AVG(o. total_amount) grouped by customer_id. Also watch for integer division in some systems; ensure numeric types support decimals if precise averages matter. Key takeaway: SUM answers 'how much' while AVG answers 'what is typical', and both depend on the set of rows you choose before aggregation.

keyIdea.title: SUM vs AVG
keyIdea.text: SUM gives total quantity, AVG gives the mean value; both depend on the filtered and grouped rows you choose.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › SUM & AVG
When to use SUM or AVG
  • SUM: cumulative totals such as revenue or quantity.
  • AVG: typical or central value such as average order value.
  • Remember to filter rows with WHERE when you want the aggregate over a subset.
SELECT
  product_category,
  SUM(sale_amount) AS total_revenue,
  AVG(sale_amount) AS avg_sale
FROM Sales
WHERE sale_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY product_category
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
Notes & gotchas

AVG only considers non-null values. If your data type is integer, AVG may perform integer division in some SQL dialects; cast to a decimal type if you need fractional results.

Key takeaway

Use SUM for totals and AVG for central values. Ensure your filters define the correct set of rows before aggregating.

screens.title: GROUP BY: how grouping shapes aggregates
screens.narratorSegment: GROUP BY divides rows into groups based on the values of one or more columns; aggregates then compute values per group. The crucial rule is that any column in SELECT that is not wrapped by an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause. The reason is simple: without grouping that column, S Q L wouldn't know which value to display for a group that contains multiple distinct values in that column. For example, if you group by product_category you can SELECT product_category and SUM(price), but you cannot SELECT product_name and SUM(price) without including product_name in GROUP BY, because product_name varies within each category. Grouping by multiple columns creates subsets that are unique combinations of those columns. A common misunderstanding is to expect S Q L to pick an arbitrary value for a non-aggregated column — most S Q L engines will error or enforce deterministic rules. Practical pattern: decide the granularity you want for your summary first, then list those columns in GROUP BY and only aggregate the remaining measures. Key takeaway: GROUP BY defines the reporting grain; align your SELECT columns with that grain to avoid errors and ambiguous results.

keyIdea.title: Grouping rule
keyIdea.text: Any non-aggregated column in SELECT must be included in GROUP BY so SQL can deterministically show one value per group.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › GROUP BY Rule
Grouping explains grain

Think of GROUP BY as choosing the reporting grain. List the columns that define each row in your summary; all other measures should be aggregates of the rows in that grain.

-- Valid: grouping by customer id and name
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spend
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name;

-- Invalid: selecting product_name without grouping by it
SELECT category, product_name, SUM(price) FROM Products GROUP BY category; -- error or ambiguous
Example scenario

If you want totals per region, GROUP BY region. If you want totals per region and city, add city to GROUP BY to get a finer grain. Always align SELECT columns with that grain.

Takeaway

Define the report grain with GROUP BY and include every non-aggregated SELECT column in that clause to avoid ambiguity.

screens.title: Order of Execution and WHERE vs HAVING
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L executes clauses in a specific logical order that affects when aggregates are available. The typical logical order is: FROM to identify tables and joins, WHERE to filter individual rows, GROUP BY to form groups, HAVING to filter groups using aggregates, SELECT to compute output expressions, and ORDER BY/LIMIT to format the final results. Because WHERE runs before GROUP BY, aggregate functions are not yet computed in WHERE and cannot be used there. That's why a condition like WHERE SUM(sales) > 1000 will error. Instead, use WHERE to narrow rows—such as filtering a date range or status—and then use HAVING to apply aggregate conditions like HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000. A useful mental model: WHERE decides which raw measurements get included in a group; HAVING inspects the group's computed metrics and decides whether to keep the group. Concrete example: to report customers with more than three orders in 2023, use WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' to include only 2023 orders, GROUP BY customer_id, and HAVING COUNT(order_id) > 3 to keep customers with many orders. Key takeaway: choose WHERE for row-level filters and HAVING for group-level aggregate filters.

keyIdea.title: Execution order
keyIdea.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. You cannot use aggregates in WHERE.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › WHERE vs HAVING
Logical order
  1. FROM — tables and joins
  2. WHERE — filter rows before grouping
  3. GROUP BY — form groups
  4. HAVING — filter groups using aggregates
  5. SELECT — calculate final expressions
  6. ORDER BY / LIMIT — format results
Example pattern
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders, SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spend
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2023-01-01' -- row-level filter
GROUP BY c.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 3 AND SUM(o.total_amount) > 500; -- group-level filter
Try moving a condition from WHERE to HAVING to see how results change: row filters affect which rows contribute to each group, while HAVING evaluates the group's aggregate outcomes.

screens.title: Filtering with WHERE vs HAVING — worked examples
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare two concrete queries that look similar but behave differently because of WHERE and HAVING placement. Suppose we want categories with total sales over 1000 but only for sales in 2023. Option A places the date filter in WHERE and the total threshold in HAVING. Option B places the date filter inside a conditional aggregate in HAVING. Option A is clear: WHERE limits rows to 2023 before grouping, GROUP BY forms categories, and HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000 filters groups. Option B attempts to filter by date using an aggregate expression inside HAVING, which is possible with conditional aggregation but is less direct and can be harder to read. Another mistake is trying to write WHERE SUM(sales) > 1000 which fails because SUM does not exist at that stage. Concrete example using Sales: write WHERE sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31', GROUP BY product_category, HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 5000. The core lesson: use WHERE for row-level constraints and HAVING for group-level aggregate constraints; conditional aggregates can be used but should be chosen deliberately. Filtering with WHERE vs HAVING — worked examples means prefer where for row-level date or status filters and having for thresholds on aggregated group metrics; conditional aggregates are an advanced alternative.. In practical terms, two queries that produce different results and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › WHERE vs HAVING Examples
Option A — WHERE then HAVING (clear)
SELECT product_category, SUM(sale_amount) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales
WHERE sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31'
GROUP BY product_category
HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 5000;
This filters rows to 2023 first, so SUM reflects only 2023 sales. HAVING then removes low-revenue categories.
Option B — conditional aggregate (advanced)
SELECT product_category,
  SUM(CASE WHEN sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31' THEN sale_amount ELSE 0 END) AS revenue_2023
FROM Sales
GROUP BY product_category
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31' THEN sale_amount ELSE 0 END) > 5000;
This keeps all rows but conditions what contributes to the aggregate. It's valid but less direct for a simple date filter.

screens.title: Example: Sales per Customer with HAVING
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a real example that combines aggregates, grouping, WHERE, and HAVING. Finally, use HAVING to filter groups by COUNT > 3 and SUM > 500. This pattern is common in customer lifecycle analysis and retention reporting. Practice by changing the date range and observing how group counts and totals change. keyIdea.text: Use WHERE for date filters, GROUP BY to set grain, and HAVING to keep only customers meeting aggregated thresholds such as order counts and spend.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sales per Customer
Full example query
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.first_name,
  c.last_name,
  COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
  SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spend,
  AVG(o.total_amount) AS average_order_value
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 3 AND SUM(o.total_amount) > 500
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
This produces a ranked list of customers who are both frequent and high spenders since the given date. Use this pattern for targeted retention or VIP lists.
Explanation cards
Row filter
WHERE limits orders to the date range so aggregates reflect that period.
Group grain

Group filter
HAVING filters customers based on aggregates like count and sum.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › PageViews Activity
Starter and solution
-- Solution: users with > 10 distinct pages, ordered by total views
SELECT
  user_id,
  COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) AS distinct_page_views,
  COUNT(page_url) AS total_page_views
FROM PageViews
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) > 10
ORDER BY total_page_views DESC;

screens.title: Common mistakes when aggregating
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes when writing aggregation queries. First, attempting to use aggregate functions inside WHERE results in an error because aggregation happens later. Second, selecting non-aggregated columns that are not in GROUP BY creates ambiguity or errors; always align SELECT columns with GROUP BY. Third, misunderstanding COUNT variants leads to incorrect metrics—COUNT(column) ignores nulls while COUNT(*) counts every row. Fourth, using DISTINCT without realizing it changes the measure from volume to uniqueness can produce surprising drops in counts. Finally, mixing filters between WHERE and HAVING without understanding their order can yield incorrect or unexpected groups. To avoid these errors, write queries in stages: run aggregates without grouping to see the global summary, add GROUP BY and confirm the grain, then add HAVING to filter groups. Use small datasets to manually verify results. A misconception to check: some learners assume HAVING is only for rare cases—it's the correct tool whenever you need to filter by aggregates. Key takeaway: follow the logical order and test queries stepwise to catch mistakes early. Common mistakes when aggregating means avoid aggregates in where, include non-aggregated select columns in group by, and choose count and distinct carefully to match your metric.. In practical terms, errors and ambiguous results to watch for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Common Pitfalls
Typical mistakes
  • Using SUM or COUNT inside WHERE (invalid): aggregates are computed after WHERE.
  • Selecting columns not in GROUP BY and not aggregated (ambiguous).
  • Mistaking COUNT(column) for COUNT(*) when NULLs exist.

screens.title: Combining multiple aggregates and grouping keys
screens.narratorSegment: Real reports often need multiple aggregates across multiple grouping keys. For example, you might compute SUM(sales), COUNT(order_id), and AVG(order_value) grouped by product_category and region to understand regional performance. The pattern is straightforward: include product_category and region in GROUP BY, compute each aggregate in SELECT with an alias, and then use HAVING to keep only groups that meet one or more aggregated thresholds. Another pattern is roll-up style summaries where you group by multiple columns to create fine-grained and coarse-grained summaries across different queries. When grouping by multiple keys, remember that the resulting grain is the unique combination of those keys—every unique pair or tuple becomes a separate group. Concrete example: GROUP BY product_category, sales_region; SELECT those keys with SUM(sale_amount) and COUNT(order_id); HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 10000 to filter high-performing combinations. A common misconception is to assume adding more grouping keys will aggregate across the first key only; instead it narrows the grain, producing more rows in the result. Key takeaway: plan your grain carefully when combining aggregates and grouping keys so each row in the result represents the intended combination. Combining multiple aggregates and grouping keys means grouping by multiple columns sets a composite grain; aggregates compute per unique combination of those keys, producing finer-grained summaries.. keyIdea.title: Multi-key grouping
keyIdea.text: Grouping by multiple columns sets a composite grain; aggregates compute per unique combination of those keys, producing finer-grained summaries.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Multi-key Grouping
Composite grouping example
SELECT
  product_category,
  sales_region,
  SUM(sale_amount) AS total_revenue,
  COUNT(order_id) AS orders
FROM Sales
GROUP BY product_category, sales_region
HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 10000
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
This produces one row per category-region combination where revenue exceeds the threshold. Adding more keys narrows groups to finer detail.
Design note

Choose grouping keys to match the report's required granularity. More keys = more rows; fewer keys = more aggregated results.

Key Takeaway

Composite GROUP BY lets you produce cross-tab like summaries by creating a unique group for each combination of keys.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three ideas capture the chapter's essentials. First, aggregate functions—COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX—produce single summary values from a set of rows; choose the function that answers your analytic question. Second, GROUP BY defines the reporting grain: any non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY so S Q L can provide a deterministic value per group. Third, HAVING filters groups after aggregation while WHERE filters rows before grouping; you cannot use aggregates in WHERE. Practice by writing queries on a Sales or PageViews table: compute global aggregates, then group by relevant keys, and finally apply HAVING to impose thresholds. Verifying results on a small sample helps catch mistakes like undercounting due to NULLs or selecting ambiguous columns. Keep these principles in mind when building reports or dashboards that rely on grouped summaries.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how S Q L turns raw rows into meaningful summaries. Aggregation is the set of techniques—COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX—that let you compress many rows into single summary values. Grouping splits rows into categories so those aggregates apply per category. Finally, HAVING lets you filter those categories using conditions on aggregate results. These tools answer questions like “what is total revenue per category?” or “which customers placed more than three orders and spent over five hundred dollars?” You will see concrete S Q L examples and a short hands-on activity using PageViews. We'll also clarify a common confusion: WHERE filters rows before aggregation, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Understanding the order of execution—FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY—helps you write correct queries and avoid errors such as trying to use SUM inside WHERE. By the end, you'll be able to produce grouped reports and choose whether a condition belongs in WHERE or HAVING. Think of aggregation as turning many measurements into the single insight that informs decisions—what summary do you need to answer your question?

By the end of this chapter you will confidently summarize data with standard aggregate functions, group rows into meaningful categories using GROUP BY, apply HAVING to filter grouped summaries, and explain when to use WHERE versus HAVING. You will be able to choose COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, or MAX based on the question you need to answer. For example, you will write queries that report total revenue per product category, count unique users per region, or find the latest event per device. We include short mnemonics and competency milestones so you can self-check: start by applying aggregates to a whole table, then group by one or more columns, then add HAVING to exclude groups that don't meet criteria. These skills matter because most analytics and reporting tasks rely on correct aggregation and grouping. Practicing the provided example queries and the PageViews task will verify that you can build grouped reports and avoid common mistakes like placing aggregate conditions in WHERE. Aim to reach the verified competency milestone by producing accurate grouped results that match the expected summaries.

This screen gives you practical validation steps. First, verify you can compute aggregates over the entire table: run COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX and check each result against known values or simple calculations. Second, test GROUP BY by grouping data by a single column and confirming that non-aggregated columns you select are listed in GROUP BY. Third, apply HAVING to exclude groups using aggregate conditions and check the counts and sums that remain. A common validation technique is to run the query without GROUP BY and then with GROUP BY on a small data subset to compare results manually. Another useful check is deliberately moving a condition between WHERE and HAVING to observe changes — for example, filter orders by date in WHERE and then require SUM(total_amount) > 500 in HAVING. These steps ensure you choose the right clause and that your aggregates reflect the intended scope of rows. Finally, reflect on one real report you build and identify which conditions are row-level and which are group-level before you write the query.

Aggregate functions compute a single summary value from multiple rows. COUNT returns the number of rows or the number of non-null values in a column; COUNT(DISTINCT) limits to unique non-null values. SUM adds numeric values and is the primary tool for totals such as total revenue. AVG gives the arithmetic mean and is useful for understanding typical values like average order value. MIN and MAX find the smallest or largest value in a set, which is helpful for earliest dates or highest prices. Use aggregates without GROUP BY when you want a single summary for the entire filtered dataset. For example, SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM Orders calculates the grand total of orders. Keep in mind null handling: COUNT(column) ignores nulls while COUNT(*) counts every row. A common misconception is thinking AVG ignores nulls differently across databases; in practice AVG operates on the non-null values present in the set. Concrete example: in a Sales table, SUM(sale_amount) gives total revenue, AVG(sale_amount) gives the average sale, and MAX(sale_date) finds the most recent sale date. Key takeaway: pick the aggregate that matches the question you ask—total, average, count, earliest, or latest.

COUNT is deceptively simple but has important variants. COUNT(*) counts every row in the result set, including rows where some columns are NULL. COUNT(column_name) counts only non-null values in that column. COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) counts unique non-null values. These differences matter when columns can be NULL or when you care about unique entities. For example, if you want to know how many orders exist, use COUNT(*) or COUNT(order_id) assuming order_id is never null; to count distinct customers who ordered, use COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). A common error is using COUNT(column) to count rows when that column can be NULL, which undercounts results. Also, using COUNT(DISTINCT) adds uniqueness semantics that can change the meaning of the metric: distinct page URLs visited versus total page views. Concrete example: in a PageViews table, COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) tells you how many different pages each user visited, while COUNT(page_url) gives total views. Key takeaway: pick the COUNT variant that captures the exact measure you want and be explicit about NULL and uniqueness semantics. COUNT variations and NULL behavior means count(*) counts rows; count(column) ignores nulls; count(distinct) counts unique non-null values—pick the one that matches your metric.. In practical terms, count(*), count(column), and count(distinct) explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SUM and AVG are the primary tools for numeric summaries. SUM adds values across rows to produce a total such as total sales or total bytes transferred. AVG computes the average of non-null values and is useful for understanding typical order sizes, session lengths, or ratings. Use SUM when you need a cumulative measure and AVG when you need a central tendency. Keep in mind that AVG's value depends on which rows are included: include or exclude rows with WHERE before grouping to change the average’s domain. A common misconception is treating AVG as resistant to outliers; it is sensitive to extreme values, so sometimes a median or trimmed average is more appropriate — though median is not a standard aggregate in every S Q L dialect. Concrete example: average order value per customer is AVG(o. total_amount) grouped by customer_id. Also watch for integer division in some systems; ensure numeric types support decimals if precise averages matter. Key takeaway: SUM answers 'how much' while AVG answers 'what is typical', and both depend on the set of rows you choose before aggregation.

GROUP BY divides rows into groups based on the values of one or more columns; aggregates then compute values per group. The crucial rule is that any column in SELECT that is not wrapped by an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause. The reason is simple: without grouping that column, S Q L wouldn't know which value to display for a group that contains multiple distinct values in that column. For example, if you group by product_category you can SELECT product_category and SUM(price), but you cannot SELECT product_name and SUM(price) without including product_name in GROUP BY, because product_name varies within each category. Grouping by multiple columns creates subsets that are unique combinations of those columns. A common misunderstanding is to expect S Q L to pick an arbitrary value for a non-aggregated column — most S Q L engines will error or enforce deterministic rules. Practical pattern: decide the granularity you want for your summary first, then list those columns in GROUP BY and only aggregate the remaining measures. Key takeaway: GROUP BY defines the reporting grain; align your SELECT columns with that grain to avoid errors and ambiguous results.

S Q L executes clauses in a specific logical order that affects when aggregates are available. The typical logical order is: FROM to identify tables and joins, WHERE to filter individual rows, GROUP BY to form groups, HAVING to filter groups using aggregates, SELECT to compute output expressions, and ORDER BY/LIMIT to format the final results. Because WHERE runs before GROUP BY, aggregate functions are not yet computed in WHERE and cannot be used there. That's why a condition like WHERE SUM(sales) > 1000 will error. Instead, use WHERE to narrow rows—such as filtering a date range or status—and then use HAVING to apply aggregate conditions like HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000. A useful mental model: WHERE decides which raw measurements get included in a group; HAVING inspects the group's computed metrics and decides whether to keep the group. Concrete example: to report customers with more than three orders in 2023, use WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' to include only 2023 orders, GROUP BY customer_id, and HAVING COUNT(order_id) > 3 to keep customers with many orders. Key takeaway: choose WHERE for row-level filters and HAVING for group-level aggregate filters.

Let's compare two concrete queries that look similar but behave differently because of WHERE and HAVING placement. Suppose we want categories with total sales over 1000 but only for sales in 2023. Option A places the date filter in WHERE and the total threshold in HAVING. Option B places the date filter inside a conditional aggregate in HAVING. Option A is clear: WHERE limits rows to 2023 before grouping, GROUP BY forms categories, and HAVING SUM(sales) > 1000 filters groups. Option B attempts to filter by date using an aggregate expression inside HAVING, which is possible with conditional aggregation but is less direct and can be harder to read. Another mistake is trying to write WHERE SUM(sales) > 1000 which fails because SUM does not exist at that stage. Concrete example using Sales: write WHERE sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31', GROUP BY product_category, HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 5000. The core lesson: use WHERE for row-level constraints and HAVING for group-level aggregate constraints; conditional aggregates can be used but should be chosen deliberately. Work through the PageViews activity. The goal is to list user_id, distinct page count, and total page views for users who visited more than ten distinct pages, ordered by total page views. The solution uses COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) to compute how many different pages each user saw and COUNT(page_url) to count total views. GROUP BY user_id produces one row per user. HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT page_url) > 10 filters to users with broad browsing behavior. ORDER BY total_page_views DESC ranks the results. This pattern shows how distinct counts and full counts serve different analytic needs: unique pages indicates breadth of engagement, while total views shows depth. There are several recurring mistakes when writing aggregation queries. First, attempting to use aggregate functions inside WHERE results in an error because aggregation happens later. Second, selecting non-aggregated columns that are not in GROUP BY creates ambiguity or errors; always align SELECT columns with GROUP BY. Third, misunderstanding COUNT variants leads to incorrect metrics—COUNT(column) ignores nulls while COUNT(*) counts every row. Fourth, using DISTINCT without realizing it changes the measure from volume to uniqueness can produce surprising drops in counts. Finally, mixing filters between WHERE and HAVING without understanding their order can yield incorrect or unexpected groups. To avoid these errors, write queries in stages: run aggregates without grouping to see the global summary, add GROUP BY and confirm the grain, then add HAVING to filter groups. Use small datasets to manually verify results. A misconception to check: some learners assume HAVING is only for rare cases—it's the correct tool whenever you need to filter by aggregates. Key takeaway: follow the logical order and test queries stepwise to catch mistakes early. Common mistakes when aggregating means avoid aggregates in where, include non-aggregated select columns in group by, and choose count and distinct carefully to match your metric.. Real reports often need multiple aggregates across multiple grouping keys. For example, you might compute SUM(sales), COUNT(order_id), and AVG(order_value) grouped by product_category and region to understand regional performance. The pattern is straightforward: include product_category and region in GROUP BY, compute each aggregate in SELECT with an alias, and then use HAVING to keep only groups that meet one or more aggregated thresholds. Another pattern is roll-up style summaries where you group by multiple columns to create fine-grained and coarse-grained summaries across different queries. When grouping by multiple keys, remember that the resulting grain is the unique combination of those keys—every unique pair or tuple becomes a separate group. Concrete example: GROUP BY product_category, sales_region; SELECT those keys with SUM(sale_amount) and COUNT(order_id); HAVING SUM(sale_amount) > 10000 to filter high-performing combinations. A common misconception is to assume adding more grouping keys will aggregate across the first key only; instead it narrows the grain, producing more rows in the result. Key takeaway: plan your grain carefully when combining aggregates and grouping keys so each row in the result represents the intended combination. Combining multiple aggregates and grouping keys means grouping by multiple columns sets a composite grain; aggregates compute per unique combination of those keys, producing finer-grained summaries.. These three ideas capture the chapter's essentials. First, aggregate functions—COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX—produce single summary values from a set of rows; choose the function that answers your analytic question. Second, GROUP BY defines the reporting grain: any non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY so S Q L can provide a deterministic value per group. Third, HAVING filters groups after aggregation while WHERE filters rows before grouping; you cannot use aggregates in WHERE. Practice by writing queries on a Sales or PageViews table: compute global aggregates, then group by relevant keys, and finally apply HAVING to impose thresholds. Verifying results on a small sample helps catch mistakes like undercounting due to NULLs or selecting ambiguous columns. Keep these principles in mind when building reports or dashboards that rely on grouped summaries.

Keep these compact reminders as a quick reference when writing aggregation queries. First, COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column): one counts rows, the other counts non-null entries—use the correct form for your metric. Second, GROUP BY defines what a row in your summary represents; always include non-aggregated columns in GROUP BY. Third, HAVING filters grouped results and may contain aggregate expressions; WHERE filters raw rows and cannot use aggregates. Before running a complex query, write the WHERE conditions you need to limit raw rows, decide the GROUP BY columns for the reporting grain, and specify HAVING conditions that reference aggregates. This simple checklist reduces errors and makes analytical queries easier to reason about.
